schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_nabadwipa.first_mention_attestation: As a Bengal Shakta Pitha in Birbhum/Katwa, Attahasa is attested in late medieval Tantric/Shakta Pitha compilations (such as the Pithanirnaya / Tantracudamani) rather than by 867 CE; the Vayu Purana (Purva Bhaga ch. 23–24) reference to Attahasa refers to a manifestation of Shiva and a Himalayan mountain, not the Bengal site.
b_nabadwipa.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Attahasa ('loud/boisterous laughter' of Shiva/Shakti). While the term appears in the Vayu Purana for a Himalayan peak and Shiva manifestation, the Bengal Shakta Pitha site of Attahasa is documented only in post-867 medieval Tantric Pitha texts.

current_repo_state.name: Attahâse
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Nabadwipa emerged after c. 1063 under the Senas; resolves via Option A to the ancient Shakta Pitha site Attahasa (Attahâse).

b_attahasa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical records; fictional Germanic-adapted ecclesiastical holding name created in the repository.

morphemes.language: Middle Low German / Old High German

b_attahasa.etymology_analysis: A fictional repository compound combining the Germanic personal name 'Ludolf' with 'munster' ('monastery, collegiate church').

b_santipura.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early 16th-century Gaudiya Vaishnava hagiographies (c. 1509 CE, Chaitanya Bhagavata / Chaitanya Charitamrita) as the residence of Advaita Acharya in Nadia.
b_santipura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'shanti' ('peace') + 'pura' ('town, city'), meaning 'city of peace'.

b_saptagrama.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 300 BCE in the Mahabharata and early Puranic literature as the sacred river Bhagirathi (the western deltaic channel of the Ganges).
b_saptagrama.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Bhagirathi' ('of Bhagiratha'), named after the legendary Ikshvaku king Bhagiratha who brought the Ganges down to earth.

b_pandua.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 1300 CE in medieval Islamic accounts and local tradition regarding the conquest of Pandua (Hooghly) by Shah Safiuddin Shahid (c. 1295–1300 CE).
b_pandua.etymology_analysis: Traditionally linked to Sanskrit/Bengali 'Pandu' or the ancient 'Pundra' ethnonym, denoting a settlement in Hooghly district.

b_kumarhati.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Kamarhati/Kumarhati in North 24 Parganas is a modern/late-medieval Bengali market settlement.

b_vijayapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 11th–12th century CE (r. Vijayasena, c. 1096–1159 CE) as the Sena capital Vijayapura in Bengal (and in Pavana-duta of Dhoyi, 12th century CE).
b_vijayapura.eponym_details: Named after Sena ruler Vijayasena (r. c. 1096–1159 CE), who established Vijayapura as his capital in Bengal.
b_vijayapura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Vijaya' ('victory', referring to King Vijayasena) + 'pura' ('city'), meaning 'city of Vijaya / victory'.

current_repo_state.name: Wîdschajapura
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from Visnupura.

b_visnupura.first_mention_attestation: Historically attested as the Malla capital Bishnupur/Vishnupur from the late 16th century CE (reign of Bir Hambir, c. 1586 CE; temple inscriptions from 17th century CE).
b_visnupura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Vishnu' (the Hindu deity) + 'pura' ('city'), meaning 'city of Vishnu'.

b_umardan.first_mention_attestation: No datable historical attestation found for Umardan in Bengal.
b_umardan.etymology_analysis: Uncertain; appears as a minor or unattested local toponym in western Bengal.

b_bikrampur.first_mention_attestation: First contemporarily attested as 'Vikramapura' in the 10th-century CE copperplate grants of the Chandra dynasty (Srichandra, r. c. 930–975 CE, e.g., Paschimbhag and Rampal copperplates).
b_bikrampur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Vikramapura', meaning 'city of valor' (or named after a royal title Vikramaditya).

b_ekdala.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 1353 CE during the Siege of Ekdala Fort by Delhi Sultan Firuz Shah Tughluq against Bengal Sultan Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah.
b_ekdala.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'ek' ('one') + 'dala' ('part, leaf, or earthen embankment'), referring to a fortified islet settlement.

b_fathabad.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a distinct river name from the late medieval period (c. 15th–16th century CE, e.g., Brihaddharma Purana and early Bengal Sultanate/European maps) as the main eastern distributary of the Ganges.
b_fathabad.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'padma' ('lotus flower'), the Bengali name for the major eastern distributary of the Ganges.

current_repo_state.name: Padmâ
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Padma River reach of the Ganges delta (in-game: Fathabad)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Late 15th-century sultanate mint town fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Padma river hydronym.

b_chandpur.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Chandpur on the Meghna-Padma confluence is attested only in late medieval/early modern Bengal records.
b_chandpur.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'Chand' ('moon' or a local figure Chand Rai/fakir) + Sanskrit/Bengali 'pur' ('town').

b_candradvipa.first_mention_attestation: First attested in 10th-century CE copperplate inscriptions of Srichandra (Rampal and Mainamati plates, c. 930–975 CE), describing his father Trailokyachandra as king of Chandradvipa.
b_candradvipa.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'chandra' ('moon') + 'dvipa' ('island'), meaning 'moon island', referring to the Barisal deltaic region.

b_bagerhat.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Khalifatabad by Khan Jahan Ali in the mid-15th century CE (c. 1450 CE); the name Bagerhat emerged in the post-Sultanate/early modern period.
b_bagerhat.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'bagh-er hat' ('market of the tiger') or 'bag-er hat' ('market of the garden'), referring to the Sundarbans-edge market town.

b_ishwaripur.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the late 16th century CE (c. 1574–1611 CE) as Jeshoreshwaripur/Ishwaripur, the capital of Raja Pratapaditya of Jessore.
b_ishwaripur.etymology_analysis: Shortened from Jeshoreshwaripur, from Sanskrit 'Ishwari' ('Goddess', referring to Jeshoreshwari Kali) + 'pura' ('town').

b_unakoti.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 7th century CE, notably by Chinese pilgrim Yijing (691 CE) as the easternmost kingdom of India ('Ho-li-ki-lo') and in 7th–8th century CE inscriptions.
b_unakoti.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized regional name 'Harikela' (literally 'sport of Hari'), denoting the ancient polity of southeastern Bengal and Chittagong.

b_tlawng.first_mention_attestation: First documented in written records in the early 19th century CE (c. 1826 CE) in British colonial reports on the Lushai Hills.
b_tlawng.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mizo hydronym for the longest river in Mizoram, known downstream in Assam as the Dhaleshwari.

b_karmanta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Karmanta-vasaka' (modern Badkamta, Comilla) in the 7th-century CE Ashrafpur copperplate inscriptions of the Khadga dynasty (c. 675 CE).
b_karmanta.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'karma' ('action, work') + 'anta' ('end, boundary'), the ancient Khadga capital in Samatata.

b_tripura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Twipra/Tripura kingdom in the Rajmala chronicle (15th century CE) and late medieval inscriptions; the Sanskritized form Tripura appears in medieval Puranic/Tantric texts.
b_tripura.etymology_analysis: From Kokborok 'Tuipra' ('near water', 'tui' + 'pra'), later Sanskritized as 'Tripura' ('three cities' or associated with Goddess Tripurasundari).

b_mainamati.first_mention_attestation: Named after Queen Mainamati (Madanavati) of the Chandra dynasty (10th–11th century CE) in medieval Bengali Nath literature (c. 11th–12th century CE); the site itself was earlier known as Pattikera/Devaparvata.
b_mainamati.eponym_details: Named after Queen Mainamati (mother of Govindachandra of the Chandra dynasty, 10th–11th century CE) in regional Nath tradition.
b_mainamati.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'Mainamati' (derived from Sanskrit 'Madanavati'), named after the legendary Chandra queen associated with the Lalmai hills.

b_udaipur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as the Manikya royal capital Rangamati on the Gomati River in the 15th century CE (under Ratna Manikya I, c. 1464 CE), before being renamed Udaipur in 1567 CE.
b_udaipur.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'ranga' ('red') + 'mati' ('earth, soil'), referring to the reddish lateritic soil of the Gomati valley.

current_repo_state.name: Rangamatî
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient Manikya royal capital Rangamati on the Gomati (in-game: Udaipur)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1567 capital of Udai Manikya fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; restored to ancient capital Rangamati.

b_devaparvata.first_mention_attestation: First epigraphically attested as 'Samatata' in the Allahabad Pillar inscription of Gupta Emperor Samudragupta (c. 350–375 CE).
b_devaparvata.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'sama' ('level, flat') + 'tata' ('shore, bank'), meaning 'level-banked (coastal deltaic) country'.

b_chatigama.first_mention_attestation: First attested in the 10th century CE in Arakanese chronicles (c. 953 CE, Tsit-ta-gong) and medieval Arab/Bengali sources as Chatigam / Chattagrama.
b_chatigama.etymology_analysis: From Prakrit/Bengali 'Chatigama' ('Chati' + 'gama' meaning 'village'), with various folk etymologies (e.g., Pir Badr's lamp 'chati' or Arakanese 'Tsit-ta-gong').

b_candranatha.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; the Chandranath Temple at Sitakunda is attested in late medieval Shakta Pitha and regional traditions.
b_candranatha.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'chandra' ('moon') + 'natha' ('lord'), an epithet of Shiva ('Lord of the Moon') worshipped at Sitakunda.

b_pattikera.first_mention_attestation: First attested in a Nepalese Buddhist manuscript dated 1015 CE (mentioning 'Pattikera') and in 11th-century CE Burmese chronicles.
b_pattikera.etymology_analysis: Medieval kingdom and city name in the Lalmai-Mainamati region of Comilla, possibly from Prakrit/Sanskrit 'patti' ('strip, settlement').

b_karnaphuli.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; the river name Karnaphuli is attested in medieval Bengali and Arakanese regional traditions.
b_karnaphuli.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'karna' ('ear') + 'phul' ('flower, earring'), meaning 'earring', from a legend of an Arakanese princess losing her earring in the river.

b_karnasubarna.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 400 BCE in Panini's Ashtadhyayi (6.2.100) and later in Kautilya's Arthashastra and the 554 CE Haraha inscription of Ishanavarman.
b_karnasubarna.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Gauda' (possibly linked to 'guda', 'jaggery/sugar', or an ancient ethnonym), denoting the core polity of western/northern Bengal.

b_raktamrittika.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 5th-century CE Sanskrit inscription of Mahanavika Buddhagupta (c. 450 CE) and in Xuanzang's Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (646 CE) as Lo-to-mo-chi (Raktamrittika Mahavihara).
b_raktamrittika.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'rakta' ('red') + 'mrittika' ('clay, earth'), meaning 'red earth' (corresponding to modern Rangamati near Karnasuvarna in Murshidabad).

b_agmahl.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 16th-century CE Mughal records (e.g., Akbarnama, c. 1592 CE) as Agmahal before Raja Man Singh I renamed it Rajmahal in 1592 CE.
b_agmahl.etymology_analysis: From 'Ag' + Persian/Arabic 'mahal' ('palace, estate'), the pre-1592 CE name of Rajmahal in Jharkhand.

b_ramavati.first_mention_attestation: First epigraphically attested as 'Kotivarsha' in the Gupta-era Damodarpur copperplate inscriptions (443–543 CE, reign of Kumaragupta I).
b_ramavati.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'koti' + 'varsha', an ancient fortified city and Gupta administrative district (vishaya) at Bangarh in Dinajpur.

b_devkot.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Devikot' / 'Devikota' in post-867 texts such as Harishena's Brihatkathakosha (931 CE) and Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharitam (c. 1100 CE).
b_devkot.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'deva'/'devi' ('deity') + 'kota' ('fort'), the medieval name of the ancient fortified city of Kotivarsha (Bangarh).

older_name_by_867.notes: Devkot (Devikota) is identified with the ancient city of Kotivarsha (modern Bangarh) attested in Gupta copperplates from 443 CE.

b_kotivarsa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in historical records; fictional Germanic-adapted collegiate church name created in the repository.
b_kotivarsa.etymology_analysis: Fictional repository name combining Low German 'Zant' ('Saint') with 'Cecilie' ('Cecilia').

current_repo_state.name: Zant-Cecilie
current_repo_state.b_origin: Zant-Cecilie — Disambiguated capital foundation: Collegiate church dedicated by Cecilie of House ThUringen

older_name_by_867.notes: Replaces the ancient barony of Kotivarsha, attested in Gupta-era Damodarpur copperplates from 443 CE.

b_laksmanavati.first_mention_attestation: Founded and attested in the late 11th century CE (c. 1080 CE, during the reign of Pala Emperor Ramapala, r. c. 1077–1130 CE, and celebrated in Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharitam).
b_laksmanavati.eponym_details: Named after Pala Emperor Ramapala (r. c. 1077–1130 CE), who founded Ramavati as his new imperial capital in Varendra.
b_laksmanavati.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Rama' (referring to Ramapala) + '-vati' (feminine suffix forming city names), meaning 'city of Ramapala'.

current_repo_state.name: Râmâwatî
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Laksmanavati was named after Laksmana Sena (r. 1178-1206, after 1171); resolves via Option A to Pala imperial seat Ramavati (Râmâwatî).

b_gaur.first_mention_attestation: The medieval city of Gaur (Lakhnauti/Lakshmanavati) in Malda is attested as an urban capital from the late 12th–early 13th century CE (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, 1205 CE onwards).
b_gaur.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Bengali form of Sanskrit 'Gauda', applied specifically to the medieval capital city in Malda district.

b_hazrat_pandua.first_mention_attestation: Attested as a major urban capital (Firuzabad / Hazrat Pandua) in Malda from 1342 CE under Sultan Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah.
b_hazrat_pandua.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'Pandua', possibly linked to 'Pundra' or 'Pandu', the Bengal Sultanate capital in Malda.

b_rampur_boalia.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Rampur Boalia' from 1825 CE when a British colonial administrative office was established there (later Rajshahi).

morphemes.translation: place of Boal fish / local village

b_rampur_boalia.etymology_analysis: Compound of two adjacent Bengali settlements, Rampur and Boalia, merged into the colonial administrative center of Rajshahi.

b_lakhnor.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 300 BCE in the Jain Acharanga Sutra (as 'Ladha') and in a 6th-century CE inscription of Devendravarman (as 'Uttara Radha').
b_lakhnor.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Radha' (Prakrit 'Ladha', modern Bengali 'Rarh'), the ancient geopolitical division of southwestern Bengal.

b_kalyaneshwari.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; the Kalyaneshwari Temple near Asansol is attested in late medieval/early modern regional records.
b_kalyaneshwari.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'kalyana' ('auspiciousness, welfare') + 'ishwari' ('goddess'), an epithet of Durga/Shakti.

b_gopbhum.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Gopbhum is attested in medieval Bengali Mangalkavya traditions (e.g., Dharmamangal) as the Sadgop territory between the Ajay and Damodar rivers.
b_gopbhum.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'gopa' ('cowherd, Sadgop') + 'bhum' ('land'), meaning 'land of the Gopas (Sadgops)'.

b_kashipur.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Kashipur in Purulia became the seat of the Panchakot Raj in the 18th century CE.

b_deogarh2.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 300 BCE in the Pali Vinaya Pitaka (fixing the eastern boundary of Aryavarta at Kajangala) and in Xuanzang's Great Tang Records (646 CE).
b_deogarh2.etymology_analysis: Ancient Sanskrit/Pali toponym 'Kajangala' denoting the territory around Rajmahal and Santhal Parganas.

current_repo_state.name: Kadschangale
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Kadschangale documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

b_shikarji.first_mention_attestation: First attested as Sammeta / Sammeda in the Jain canonical text Jnatrdharmakatha (compiled c. 5th century CE, c. 450 CE), prior to the later Hindi honorific suffix '-jī' in Shikharji.
b_shikarji.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'shikhara' ('peak, summit') + honorific '-ji', meaning 'Venerable Peak'.

b_koriya.first_mention_attestation: First attested as 'Jharikhanda' in a 13th-century CE copperplate inscription of Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva II (c. 1295 CE) and later in the Akbarnama (c. 1590s CE).
b_koriya.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Prakrit 'jhari' ('forest, bush') + 'khanda' ('land, region'), meaning 'land of forests'.

b_ambikapur.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Ambikapur developed as the capital of Surguja in the modern/late medieval period.
b_ambikapur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Ambika' (a name of Goddess Durga) + 'pura' ('town').

b_beohari.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 16th century CE (c. 1550 CE), founded by members of the Beohar lineage who served as ministers and jagirdars of the Gond kingdom under Rani Durgavati.
b_beohari.eponym_details: Named after the Beohar title/lineage, hereditary prime ministers and jagirdars of the Gond kingdom (16th century CE) who founded settlements named Beohari.
b_beohari.etymology_analysis: Derived from the title 'Beohar' (from Sanskrit 'vyavahari', 'administrator/minister'), denoting a settlement founded by a Beohar.

b_rajrappa.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; the Chhinnamasta temple and pilgrimage site at Rajrappa are attested in early modern/colonial records.
b_rajrappa.etymology_analysis: Local Jharkhandi toponym of uncertain etymology for the sacred waterfall and Chhinnamasta temple site at the confluence of the Damodar and Bhairavi rivers.

b_kenduli.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the late 12th century CE (c. 1170 CE) in the Gita Govinda of poet Jayadeva as 'Kendubilva', his birthplace.
b_kenduli.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Kendubilva' ('kendu' + 'bilva' trees), contracted in Bengali to 'Kenduli'.

b_rohtas.first_mention_attestation: While a 7th-century CE seal matrix of Shashanka was found at the site, the name 'Rohtas' (Rohitasva) is first epigraphically attested in 12th-century CE Khayaravala inscriptions (Pratapadhavala, 1158–1169 CE, and Shri Pratapa, 1222 CE).
b_rohtas.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Sanskrit 'Rohitashva-giri' / 'Rohitashva-durga', named after the legendary prince Rohitashva, son of King Harishchandra.

b_betla.first_mention_attestation: No datable pre-867 CE attestation; Betla is a modern village and national park name in Latehar/Palamu, Jharkhand.

morphemes.translation: village toponym (or modern acronym for Bison, Elephant, Tiger, Leopard, Axis-deer)

b_betla.etymology_analysis: Local village name in Latehar district, Jharkhand (also popularly backronymed for wildlife in Betla National Park).

b_palamau.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the early 17th century CE (c. 1613 CE) as the Chero dynasty stronghold of Palamu (Palamau) under Bhagwant Rai.

morphemes.translation: regional name (possibly 'place of frost' or 'eighteen forts')

b_palamau.etymology_analysis: Regional name of uncertain indigenous/Dravidian or Munda origin (variously glossed as 'place of frost' or from 'pala'/'mu').

b_gaya.first_mention_attestation: Attested from c. 500 BCE in Yaska's Nirukta (referencing Gaya), early Buddhist texts, and Ashoka's Major Rock Edict VIII (c. 256 BCE, Sambodhi/Bodh Gaya).
b_gaya.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Gaya', named in Vedic and Puranic tradition after the asura/sage Gayasura.

b_bodh_gaya.first_mention_attestation: The modern compound name 'Bodh Gaya' came into use in the 18th century CE (previously known as Uruvela, Sambodhi, Vajrasana, and Mahabodhi).
b_bodh_gaya.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit/Pali 'bodhi' (enlightenment, referring to Gautama Buddha's awakening under the Bodhi Tree) combined with 'Gaya' (the adjacent ancient city). The compound 'Bodh Gaya' emerged in the 18th century CE to distinguish the Buddhist pilgrimage site from Hindu Gaya.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ashoka's Major Rock Edict No. 8 (c. 250 BCE, as 'Sambodhi'); early Pali Canon ('Uruvela').
older_name_by_867.notes: Known as Uruvela in early Buddhist texts and as Sambodhi ('Complete Enlightenment') in Ashoka's 3rd-century BCE Rock Edict No. 8.

b_kukkutapada.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Kukkutapadagiri' in the 2nd-century CE Sanskrit Buddhist text Ashokavadana, and later recorded by Chinese pilgrim Faxian (c. 400 CE) and Xuanzang (7th century CE).
b_kukkutapada.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Kukkutapada' (literally 'Cock's Foot', short for Kukkutapadagiri, 'Cock's Foot Mountain'), referring to the three-peaked hill (modern Gurpa Hill or Kurkihar) associated with Mahakasyapa in Buddhist tradition.

b_pataliputra.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Atharvaveda (c. 1000 BCE) as the name of the eastern people and region of Magadha.

morphemes.translation: ancient eastern kingdom and its inhabitants

b_pataliputra.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Magadha', the Vedic and classical name of the kingdom and region in southern Bihar. The active repository name 'Magadhe' is an adaptation of 'Magadha'.

b_odantapuri.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Buddhist mahavihara by Pala Emperor Gopala I (r. c. 750–770 CE) or his son Dharmapala in the mid-to-late 8th century CE.
b_odantapuri.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Odantapuri' (also rendered 'Uddandapura'), meaning 'lofty city' or 'high citadel', referring to the celebrated Pala-era Buddhist monastic university located at modern Bihar Sharif.

b_rajagrha.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Buddhist Pali texts (as 'Rajagaha', c. 5th century BCE) and the Mahabharata as the first capital of Magadha.
b_rajagrha.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Rajagrha' (Pali 'Rajagaha'), meaning 'abode of kings' or 'royal city', the early capital of Magadha (modern Rajgir).

b_maner.first_mention_attestation: First gains historical prominence in the 13th century CE through its association with Sufi saint Makhdoom Yahya Maneri; no pre-867 CE written attestation is documented.
b_maner.etymology_analysis: Modern town name in Patna district, Bihar (also known as Maner Sharif). Its pre-medieval etymology is uncertain, and its recorded history begins in the 13th century CE as a Sufi center.

b_bihar_sharif.first_mention_attestation: The name 'Bihar' (from Sanskrit 'vihara') is attested in Minhaj-i-Siraj's Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (1260 CE) describing Bakhtiyar Khalji's c. 1200 CE conquest; 'Sharif' was added later for its Sufi shrines.
b_bihar_sharif.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit 'vihara' (monastery, referring to the Odantapuri mahavihara) combined with Arabic/Persian 'sharif' (noble), reflecting its later status as a Sufi center.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Founded by Pala Emperor Gopala I (r. c. 750–770 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Bihar Sharif occupies the site of the ancient Odantapuri (Uddandapura) Buddhist monastic university.

b_mudgagiri.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested as 'Mudgagiri' in the Munger (Monghyr) Copperplate Inscription of Pala Emperor Devapala, issued in his 33rd regnal year (c. 843 CE).
b_mudgagiri.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Mudgagiri' ('hill of mudga'), the early medieval name of modern Munger in Bihar, used as a royal military camp by the Pala dynasty.

b_campa.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Buddhist Pali texts (such as the Digha Nikaya, c. 5th century BCE) and the Mahabharata as the capital of the Anga Mahajanapada.
b_campa.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Campa' (or Champa), named either after the champaca tree or the adjacent Champa River; the ancient capital of Anga near modern Bhagalpur.

b_vikramasila.first_mention_attestation: Founded by Pala Emperor Dharmapala (r. c. 783–820 CE) in the late 8th or early 9th century CE as a major Buddhist monastic university.
b_vikramasila.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Vikramasila', combining 'vikrama' (valor, echoing Dharmapala's title Vikramasila) and 'sila' (virtue/conduct).

b_sasaram.first_mention_attestation: Derived from Sanskrit 'Sahasrarama' ('one thousand groves'); while an Ashokan Minor Rock Edict (c. 250 BCE) stands nearby, the modern name 'Sasaram' is post-medieval with no dated pre-867 CE attestation.
b_sasaram.etymology_analysis: Evolved from Sanskrit 'Sahasrarama' ('one thousand groves/monasteries') via 'Sahasram' into modern Hindi/Bhojpuri 'Sasaram'.

b_jaund.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1492 CE during the Lodi-Sharqi War as the fort of Jaund (Chaund) near Bhabhua where Husain Shah Sharqi took refuge.
b_jaund.etymology_analysis: Vernacular toponym for a medieval fort (also spelled Chaund) in the Kaimur/Bhabhua region of western Bihar, attested in late 15th-century CE Sultanate chronicles.

b_arrah.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Aramnagar' in Jain inscriptions at nearby Masarh dated Samvat 1443 (1386 CE), and as 'Ari'/'Are' in Babur's Baburnama (1529 CE).
b_arrah.etymology_analysis: Derived either from Sanskrit 'Aramnagar' ('city of groves', attested in 1386 CE Masarh inscriptions) or from Sanskrit 'Aranya' ('forest'), reflecting the formerly forested terrain of Bhojpur.

b_bishnupur.first_mention_attestation: While Malla dynastic chronicles trace the kingdom to Adi Malla (c. 694 CE), contemporary historical attestation of 'Mallabhum' dates to the late medieval/Mughal period (16th century CE).
b_bishnupur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'Mallabhum' ('Land of the Mallas'), referring to the kingdom ruled by the Malla kings of Bishnupur in Bankura, West Bengal.

b_baghmundi.first_mention_attestation: Modern village and administrative block in Purulia district, West Bengal, with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_baghmundi.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Bengali/tribal toponym in Purulia district, meaning 'tiger head' or 'tiger hill', with no attested pre-medieval written record.

b_midnapore.first_mention_attestation: Contemporarily attested in the Midnapore copperplate inscriptions of Gauda king Shashanka (first half of the 7th century CE, c. 600–625 CE).
b_midnapore.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Dandabhukti', an ancient and early medieval administrative province ('bhukti') in the Rarh region of Bengal/Odisha, attested in 7th-century CE copperplates of Shashanka.

current_repo_state.name: Dandabukti
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English spelling Midnapore; resolves via Option A to ancient Gupta/Shashanka province Dandabhukti (b_dantan).

b_dantan.first_mention_attestation: Modern vernacular name derived from the ancient province of Dandabhukti; no datable pre-867 CE attestation of the shortened form 'Dantan' exists.
b_dantan.etymology_analysis: Modern Bengali toponym in Paschim Medinipur preserving the name of the ancient and early medieval region of Dandabhukti.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Midnapore copperplates of Shashanka (early 7th century CE, c. 600–625 CE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Dantan preserves the name of Dandabhukti, attested in 7th-century CE Gauda inscriptions.

b_tamralipti.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (77 CE, as 'Taluctae'), Ptolemy's Geographica (c. 150 CE, as 'Tamalities'), as well as early Buddhist literature and the Mahabharata.
b_tamralipti.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Tamralipti' (also 'Tamralipta'), meaning 'copper-coated', the ancient maritime port city in Bengal corresponding to modern Tamluk.

b_sagardwip.first_mention_attestation: The modern Bengali island name 'Sagardwip' has no datable pre-867 CE attestation, though the sacred confluence ('Gangasagarasangam') is mentioned in the Mahabharata.
b_sagardwip.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'Sagar' (ocean/sea, also linked to King Sagara) + 'dwip' (island), meaning 'Ocean Island' at the mouth of the Hooghly River.

older_name_by_867.notes: The sacred confluence Gaṅgāsāgarasaṅgama is attested in the Mahabharata prior to the modern Bengali island name Sagardwip.

b_chatrabhog.first_mention_attestation: Attested in Bipradas Pipilai's Bengali Manasavijaya (1495 CE) and Chaitanya Bhagavata (early 16th century CE) as a riverine settlement along the old Bhagirathi channel.
b_chatrabhog.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'Chhatra' (umbrella/parasol) and 'bhoga' (offering/estate), a historic riverside pilgrimage site in South 24 Parganas, West Bengal.

b_chandraketugarh.first_mention_attestation: Although the archaeological site dates back to the 3rd century BCE, the modern name 'Chandraketugarh' is a post-medieval/modern folk designation with no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_chandraketugarh.etymology_analysis: Named after a legendary local king Chandraketu combined with 'garh' (fort). Archaeologically, the site flourished from the Mauryan through Gupta periods and is widely identified with classical Gange.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Ptolemy's Geographica (c. 150 CE) as Gange, capital of Gangaridai.
older_name_by_867.notes: Scholars widely identify the ancient port city at Chandraketugarh with Gange, capital of Gangaridai in Ptolemy's Geographica.

b_bangaon.first_mention_attestation: The modern Hindi river name 'Burhi Gandak' ('Old Gandak') has no datable pre-867 CE attestation.
b_bangaon.etymology_analysis: From Hindi 'burhi' (old) + 'Gandak' (from Sanskrit 'Gandaki'), designating an old paleochannel of the Gandaki River in northern Bihar.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Megasthenes' Indica (c. 300 BCE, as 'Kondochates') and the Mahabharata (as 'Gandaki').
older_name_by_867.notes: Burhi Gandak is an old channel of the Gandaki River system, attested in antiquity as Gandaki / Kondochates.

b_jalalghar.first_mention_attestation: Built in 1722 CE by Saif Khan, the Faujdar of Purnea, as a frontier fort.
b_jalalghar.eponym_details: Named after Saif Khan (birth name Saif-ud-Din Jalal Khan), Faujdar of Purnea, who built Jalalgarh ('Jalal's Fort') in 1722 CE.
b_jalalghar.etymology_analysis: Compound of Arabic/Persian 'Jalal' and Hindi 'garh' (fort), denoting the 18th-century CE frontier fortress north of Purnia, Bihar.

b_burhi_gandak.first_mention_attestation: A German-language/Christianized adaptation in the repository ('Kunigundeszelle'), referencing Saint Cunigunde of Luxembourg (c. 975–1033 CE, canonized 1200 CE); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_burhi_gandak.eponym_details: Named after Saint Cunigunde (Kunigunde) of Luxembourg (c. 975–1033 CE, canonized 1200 CE), Empress of the Holy Roman Empire.
b_burhi_gandak.etymology_analysis: German compound meaning 'Kunigunde's cell/hermitage', a repository adaptation of the Bihar barony 'b_burhi_gandak' named after post-867 CE Saint Cunigunde of Luxembourg.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Megasthenes, Indica (c. 300 BCE, as Kondochates) and Mahabharata (as Gaṇḍakī)
older_name_by_867.notes: The fictional Germanicized name Kunigundeszelle sits on the Burhi Gandak / Gandaki river slot, whose classical hydronym Kondochates / Gaṇḍakī is attested by c. 300 BCE (matching neighboring b_bangaon).

b_kusinagara.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Buddhist Pali texts (as 'Kusinara', c. 5th century BCE) and Sanskrit texts (as 'Kusinagara') as the place of Gautama Buddha's parinirvana.
b_kusinagara.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Kusinagara' (Pali 'Kusinara'), meaning 'city of kusha grass' (or of King Kusa), one of the four major Buddhist pilgrimage sites.

b_pava.first_mention_attestation: Attested in early Buddhist Pali texts (Digha Nikaya, c. 5th century BCE) and Jain texts (as 'Pava' / 'Pavapuri') as a Malla capital where the Buddha ate his last meal.
b_pava.etymology_analysis: From Pali/Sanskrit 'Pava', an ancient city of the Malla confederacy located near Kushinagar (often identified with modern Fazilnagar/Padrauna).

b_chapra.first_mention_attestation: Modern town in Saran district, Bihar, first gaining prominence in the 17th–18th centuries CE as a Dutch/European saltpeter trading center; no pre-867 CE attestation.
b_chapra.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Hindi/Bhojpuri toponym ('Chhapra', rendered 'Tschapra' in the repository), administrative headquarters of Saran district in Bihar.

b_mithila.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Shatapatha Brahmana (c. 8th–6th century BCE) and the Ramayana/Mahabharata as the capital city and kingdom of Videha.

morphemes.translation: ancient city and region of King Mithi

b_mithila.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Mithila', traditionally linked to King Mithi (Janaka) of Videha, attested in late Vedic literature as the principal city and cultural region of northern Bihar.

b_sugauna.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 14th–15th century CE as a capital of the Oiniwar (Sugauna) dynasty of Mithila; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_sugauna.etymology_analysis: Maithili village name in Madhubani district, Bihar, which gave its alternate name ('Sugauna dynasty') to the medieval Oiniwar rulers of Mithila.

b_darbhanga.first_mention_attestation: Medieval and modern city in Bihar (part of Sarkar Tirhut under the Mughals); no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_darbhanga.etymology_analysis: Popularly derived from 'Dwar-Banga' / 'Dar-e-Banga' ('gateway to Bengal') or an unverified founder 'Darbhangi Khan'; neither etymology is attested before the late medieval period.

b_hajipur.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1350 CE by Bengal Sultan Haji Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah, after whom the town is named.
b_hajipur.eponym_details: Named after Haji Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah (r. 1342–1358 CE), founder of the Bengal Sultanate, who established the city c. 1350 CE.

morphemes.translation: title of Ilyas Shah (pilgrim to Mecca)

b_hajipur.etymology_analysis: Hybrid Arabic/Persian-Sanskrit compound meaning 'city of Haji (Ilyas Shah)', founded in the mid-14th century CE in Vaishali district, Bihar.

b_simaramapura.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1097 CE (or late 11th century CE) by King Nanyadeva of the Karnata dynasty of Mithila as his fortified capital.
b_simaramapura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Simaramapura' (modern Simraungadh in southeastern Nepal on the Bihar border), the 11th-century CE capital of the Karnata dynasty of Mithila.

b_kesaria.first_mention_attestation: While the Kesaria Stupa dates to the Maurya–Gupta periods and Xuanzang (7th century CE) noted a stupa at 'Kia-shi-po-lo', the modern town name 'Kesaria' has no datable pre-867 CE attestation.
b_kesaria.etymology_analysis: Modern Hindi/Bhojpuri town name in East Champaran, Bihar, famous for its monumental Buddhist stupa.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Xuanzang, Great Tang Records on the Western Regions (646 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Xuanzang (646 CE) recorded the stupa at Kia-shi-po-lo (identified with Kesaputta / Kesaria) prior to the modern town name Kesaria.

b_barohiya.first_mention_attestation: Modern village in Chanpatia block, West Champaran district, Bihar, with no datable historical or pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_barohiya.etymology_analysis: Modern vernacular village name in Pashchim Champaran, Bihar, with no documented pre-modern history.

b_madhupur.first_mention_attestation: Modern town and upazila in Tangail district, Bangladesh (and Madhupur Garh forest tract); no datable pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_madhupur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'Madhu' (honey) + 'pur' (town), meaning 'city of honey', a modern administrative center in central Bangladesh.

b_pabna.first_mention_attestation: Modern city on the Padma River in Bangladesh (constituted as a district headquarters in the 19th century CE); no datable pre-867 CE written attestation exists.
b_pabna.etymology_analysis: Modern Bengali city name in west-central Bangladesh; sometimes linked in local tradition to 'Padma' or 'Pundra', but without confirmed pre-modern attestation.

b_somapur.first_mention_attestation: Built by Pala Emperor Dharmapala (r. c. 783–820 CE) and attested on terracotta monastic seals from the site reading 'Sri-Somapure-Sri-Dharmapaladeva-Mahavihariy-aryabhikshu-sanghasya'.
b_somapur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Somapura' ('Moon City'), referring to Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur in Naogaon, Bangladesh, founded by Dharmapala.

b_pundravardhana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Pundravardhana' in the 2nd-century CE Ashokavadana (c. 150 CE), with the Pundra people attested earlier in 7th–8th century BCE Vedic texts and Pundranagara in the 3rd-century BCE Mahasthan Brahmi Inscription.
b_pundravardhana.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Pundravardhana' ('prospering land of the Pundras'), the ancient kingdom and Gupta-era bhukti in northern Bengal.

b_mahasthangarh.first_mention_attestation: The modern Bengali compound name 'Mahasthangarh' ('great-place fort') is post-medieval; the ancient city at the site was called Pundranagara.
b_mahasthangarh.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Bengali 'Mahasthan' ('great place') + 'garh' (fort), the modern name for the ruins of ancient Pundranagara in Bogra district, Bangladesh.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Mahasthan Brahmi Inscription (c. 3rd century BCE, c. 250 BCE).
older_name_by_867.notes: Mahasthangarh is the archaeological site of Pundranagara, attested in the 3rd-century BCE Mahasthan Brahmi Inscription.

b_ghoraghat.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the late 15th century CE (by 1474 CE) as a frontier garrison of the Bengal Sultanate associated with Shah Ismail Ghazi under Sultan Ruknuddin Barbak Shah.
b_ghoraghat.etymology_analysis: From Bengali 'ghora' (horse) + 'ghat' (riverbank landing/crossing), a medieval Sultanate and Mughal frontier outpost in Dinajpur, Bangladesh.

b_suvarnagram.first_mention_attestation: Attested as 'Suvarnagrama' in the mid-13th century CE when Deva dynasty King Dasharathadeva shifted his capital there from Bikrampur (and Muslim settlers arrived c. 1281 CE).
b_suvarnagram.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Suvarnagrama' ('golden village'), the medieval Sanskritic form of Sonargaon in Bangladesh.

b_bokainagar.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 15th-century CE tradition: either built by a 15th-century Koch chieftain named Bokai or by Majlis Khan Humayun under Sultan Saifuddin Firuz Shah II (r. 1486–1489 CE).
b_bokainagar.eponym_details: Named after a 15th-century CE Koch tribal chieftain named Bokai, who according to local tradition built the fort and gave it his name.
b_bokainagar.etymology_analysis: Compound of the personal name 'Bokai' (a 15th-century CE Koch chieftain) and Bengali/Sanskrit 'nagar' (town/fort), located in Gauripur Upazila, Mymensingh, Bangladesh.

b_dhakeshwari_jatiya_mandir.first_mention_attestation: Built in the 12th century CE (c. 1100 CE) by Sena dynasty King Ballal Sen; 'Jatiya Mandir' ('National Temple') is a modern 20th-century designation.
b_dhakeshwari_jatiya_mandir.etymology_analysis: From Bengali/Sanskrit 'Dhakeshwari' (Goddess of Dhaka) + 'Jatiya Mandir' (National Temple), the 12th-century CE Sena-era temple in Dhaka, Bangladesh.

current_repo_state.name: Dhakeschwari Jatiya Mandir
current_repo_state.b_origin: Dhakeschwari Jatiya Mandir (constituent holding of Suwarnagrâm)

b_nasirabad.first_mention_attestation: The river name 'Brahmaputra' ('Son of Brahma') is first attested in the 10th-century CE Kalika Purana (c. 950–1000 CE); earlier texts and inscriptions refer to the river as 'Lauhitya'.
b_nasirabad.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Brahmaputra' ('son of Brahma'), the major river flowing through Assam and Bangladesh, which replaced the older Sanskrit hydronym 'Lauhitya' in the 10th-century CE Kalika Purana.

current_repo_state.name: Brahmapûtra
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient sacred Brahmaputra River reach (in-game: Nasirabad)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 19th-century colonial town fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Brahmaputra river hydronym.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Markandeya Purana (c. 3rd–6th century CE), Mahabharata, and Kamarupa copperplate inscriptions.
older_name_by_867.notes: Lauhitya/Lohitya was the standard Sanskrit name for the Brahmaputra River prior to the 10th-century CE Kalika Purana.

b_chutia.first_mention_attestation: Ethnonym of the Austroasiatic-speaking Munda people of Chotanagpur/Jharkhand; no datable pre-867 CE written attestation of 'Munda' as a territorial/barony name exists.
b_chutia.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Munda people of Jharkhand (from Sanskrit/Mundari 'munda', originally meaning 'headman' or 'village chief').

b_ratu.first_mention_attestation: The Nagvanshi rulers shifted their capital from Palkot to Ratu in 1870 CE (with Ratu Palace built 1899–1901 CE); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_ratu.etymology_analysis: Modern town and former Nagvanshi seat near Ranchi, Jharkhand, established as the Nagvanshi capital in 1870 CE.

b_chauragarh.first_mention_attestation: Built by Gond King Sangram Shah (r. 1488–1541 CE) in the early 16th century CE (and besieged by Mughal forces in 1564 CE).
b_chauragarh.etymology_analysis: From Hindi 'Chaura' + 'garh' (fort), the early 16th-century CE Gond hill fortress in Narsinghpur district, Madhya Pradesh.

b_barman.first_mention_attestation: Attested in 1825 CE colonial records of Narsinghpur district when Chawarpatha and Tendukheda were transferred; no pre-867 CE attestation exists.
b_barman.etymology_analysis: From Hindi 'tendu' (the tendu/ebony leaf tree) + 'kheda' (hamlet/village), a modern town in Narsinghpur district, Madhya Pradesh.

b_hoshangabad.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (c. 80 CE, as 'Nammadios'), Ptolemy's Geographica (c. 150 CE, as 'Namadus'), and the Mahabharata and Puranas.
b_hoshangabad.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Narmada' ('giver of pleasure'), the sacred west-flowing river of central India, attested in 1st-century CE Greco-Roman and Sanskrit sources.

current_repo_state.name: Narmadâ
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient sacred Narmada River reach (in-game: Hoshangabad)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: 1405 fortress of Hoshang Shah fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient sacred Narmada hydronym.

b_handia.first_mention_attestation: Prosperous Mughal-era town (sarkar headquarters captured by the Marathas in 1742 CE and mentioned in the 1759 CE Chahar Gulshan); no pre-867 CE attestation exists.

morphemes.translation: historic river crossing town on the Narmada

b_handia.etymology_analysis: Vernacular Hindi toponym (rendered 'Handje' in the repository) on the southern bank of the Narmada River in Harda district, Madhya Pradesh, prominent during the Mughal period.

b_tripuri.first_mention_attestation: Attested on city-state coins from Tewar dated to the late 3rd or 2nd century BCE, and later as the capital of the Kalachuris of Tripuri from the 8th century CE.
b_tripuri.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit 'Tripuri' ('three cities'), the ancient capital of the Chedi/Dahala region near modern Tewar (Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh).

b_mandla.first_mention_attestation: Attested from the 16th century CE as part of the Garha-Mandla Gond kingdom; no pre-867 CE written attestation exists.

morphemes.translation: circle, district, loop of the Narmada

b_mandla.etymology_analysis: Derived from Sanskrit/Hindi 'mandala' (circle or administrative district, possibly referring to the river bend of the Narmada enclosing the town), a Gond capital in Madhya Pradesh.

b_banjar.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-modern written sources; modern/vernacular toponym derived from the Banjar River, a tributary of the Narmada in Mandla district, Madhya Pradesh.

morphemes.translation: Banjar River hydronym (traditionally linked to barren/forestland or Banjara trade routes)

b_banjar.etymology_analysis: Derived directly from the Banjar River, a major southern tributary joining the Narmada at Mandla in central India (cf. Bamhani Banjar).

b_bohani.first_mention_attestation: First documented in the 1906 CE Narsinghpur District Gazetteer compiled by R. V. Russell, which notes its earlier traditional name Kohani and local traditions of a 12th-century CE tank.

morphemes.translation: village toponym (evolved from earlier local form Kohani)

b_bohani.etymology_analysis: Modern Hindi village name in Narsinghpur district, Madhya Pradesh; the 1906 CE Narsinghpur District Gazetteer records an earlier undated local name Kohani, with no confirmed pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_moti_mahal.first_mention_attestation: Constructed between 1651 CE and 1667 CE by the Garha-Mandla Gond ruler Hirde Shah at Ramnagar, Mandla district.
b_moti_mahal.etymology_analysis: Compound of Hindi motī ('pearl') and mahal ('palace', ultimately from Arabic maḥall), meaning 'Pearl Palace', built in the mid-17th century CE under Gond king Hirde Shah.

b_bandhugadha.first_mention_attestation: The Bandhavgarh hill caves preserve Brahmi inscriptions of the Magha kings from the 2nd–3rd century CE, though the Sanskritized fort name Bandhugadha (Bandhavgarh) itself lacks a datable pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_bandhugadha.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit bandhu ('brother, kinsman') and gaḍha ('fort'), traditionally interpreted as 'Brother's Fort' in reference to the Ramayana legend of Rama gifting the fort to Lakshmana; rendered in-repo as Bândûgade (Bāndhūgadha).

b_bahoriband.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1125 CE (Vikram Samvat 1182) Bahoriband stone inscription on the colossal Shantinath Jain statue from the reign of Kalachuri king Gayakarna.
b_bahoriband.etymology_analysis: Vernacular compound (also spelled Bahuriband / Bahulaband) meaning 'many embankments', referring to the numerous ancient rainwater-harvesting dams and reservoirs extending north toward Tigawa; Cunningham's 1879 CE identification with Ptolemy's Tholabana is conjectural.

b_soubhagyapura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; Sanskritized form of Sohagpur (Shahdol district, Madhya Pradesh), where the surviving Virateshwar Shiva temple dates to the 11th-century CE Kalachuri period.
b_soubhagyapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound saubhāgya ('good fortune, auspiciousness') + pura ('city'), functioning as the Sanskritized counterpart to Sohagpur in Shahdol district (later associated in Baghel dynastic tradition with Maharaja Sohag Deo).

b_ratanpur.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Ratnapura in the 1114 CE Ratanpur stone inscription of Jajalladeva I, recording its foundation by his grandfather Ratnadeva I (r. c. 1045–1065 CE).
b_ratanpur.eponym_details: Named after Kalachuri king Ratnadeva I (alias Ratnaraja, r. c. 1045–1065 CE), who established Ratnapura as the capital of the Ratnapura Kalachuri dynasty.

morphemes.translation: jewel (personal name element of Ratnadeva I)

b_ratanpur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Ratnapura ('City of Ratna' / 'Jewel City'), named after its 11th-century CE founder Ratnadeva I of the Kalachuris of Ratnapura.

b_savarinarayana.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the 1127 CE (Kalachuri Era 878) Seorinarayan copperplate grant of Ratnadeva II and the 1146 CE (Kalachuri Era 898) Sheorinarayan statue inscription.

morphemes.translation: Shabari (devotee of Rama in the Ramayana)

b_savarinarayana.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Śabarī-Nārāyaṇa (modern Shivrinarayan / Sheorinarayan), commemorating the Ramayana episode in which the ascetic Shabari offered berries to Rama (Vishnu/Narayana).

b_pali.first_mention_attestation: Attested in the undated sanctum-door inscription of Bana king Vikramaditya I (r. c. 870–900 CE) at the Pali Shiva temple, and in the 10th-century CE Bilhari stone inscription recording its capture by Shankaragana II (r. c. 890–910 CE).
b_pali.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Prakrit pallī or pāli ('settlement, village'), attested in late 9th-century CE Bana and Tripuri Kalachuri epigraphy in Korba district, Chhattisgarh.

b_tummana.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Tummāṇa in the 1114 CE Ratanpur stone inscription of Jajalladeva I, which records that Kalingaraja established it as his capital around 1000 CE.
b_tummana.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized regional toponym Tummāṇa (modern Tuman in Korba/Bilaspur region, Chhattisgarh), founded as the first Dakshina Kosala capital of the Ratnapura Kalachuris by Kalingaraja c. 1000 CE.

b_amarkantak.first_mention_attestation: Mentioned as Amarakūṭa by Kalidasa (c. 4th–5th century CE) and as Amarakaṇṭaka in the Matsya, Kurma, and Vayu Puranas (compiled c. 3rd–7th century CE).
b_amarkantak.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit amarakaṇṭaka (amara 'immortal' + kaṇṭaka 'thorn/peak'), attested earlier in Kalidasa's poetry as Amarakūṭa ('immortal peak'), referring to the sacred Maikal plateau mountain where the Narmada and Son rivers rise.

b_haruppeswara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Hārūppeśvara in the 829 CE (Gupta Era 510) Hayunthal copperplate and Tezpur rock inscription of Harjaravarman, as well as the 9th-century CE Tezpur plates of Vanamalavarmadeva.
b_haruppeswara.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized Mlechchha/Salastambha capital name Hārūppeśvara (also Haḍapeśvara; modern Tezpur, Assam), incorporating īśvara ('lord', referring to the dynasty's tutelary Shiva shrine Hetuka-Śūlin).

b_numaligarh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; nearby Deopahar preserves 9th–12th century CE stone temple ruins, while the Assamese name Numaligarh dates to the later medieval/Ahom period.
b_numaligarh.etymology_analysis: Assamese compound of Numalī and gaṛh ('fort'), located in Golaghat district, Assam, adjacent to the Deopahar archaeological site.

b_narayanpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; historically prominent from the late 15th century CE as the birthplace of Neo-Vaishnavite saint Madhavdeva (b. 1489 CE) in Lakhimpur district, Assam.
b_narayanpur.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Assamese Nārāyaṇa ('Vishnu') + pur ('town'), meaning 'Town of Narayana'.

b_kamarupanagara.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kāmarūpanagara from the 11th century CE under Kamarupa Pala king Dharmapala (r. c. 1035–1060 CE), who established his capital at North Guwahati.
b_kamarupanagara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Kāmarūpa-nagara ('City of Kamarupa'), the 11th-century CE capital city established by Dharmapala at North Guwahati (distinct from the 4th-century CE regional name Kāmarūpa).

b_manikuta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Maṇikūṭa in the Kalika Purana (c. 10th–11th century CE), corresponding to the 10th-century CE Pala-era temple ruins on Monikut Hill in Hajo, Assam.
b_manikuta.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit maṇikūṭa ('Jewel Peak'), the sacred hill (Manikuta Parvata / Monikut) in Hajo, Assam, where the Hayagriva Madhava Temple stands.

b_pragyotisapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Prāgjyotiṣa in local Kamarupa inscriptions from the 7th century CE (Bhaskaravarman) and explicitly in the city form Prāgjyotiṣapura by the 9th century CE.
b_pragyotisapura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Prāgjyotiṣapura ('City of Eastern Astrology/Light'), the ancient capital of the Varman dynasty of Kamarupa at modern Guwahati.

b_dhubri.first_mention_attestation: Documented in early modern historical accounts such as Guru Tegh Bahadur's visit in 1669 CE and British colonial records (municipal board 1883 CE); no pre-867 CE written attestation.

morphemes.translation: toponym traditionally linked to Netai Dhubuni (washerwoman)

b_dhubri.etymology_analysis: Assamese river-port toponym on the Brahmaputra in western Assam, traditionally associated with the legend of Netai Dhubuni Ghat.

b_kamatapur.first_mention_attestation: The fortified city at Bhitagarh in Panchagarh, Bangladesh, dates archaeologically to the 5th–6th century CE, but the Bengali name Bhitagarh ('Inner Fort') is a modern/vernacular designation with no contemporary pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_kamatapur.etymology_analysis: Bengali compound bhitar ('inner') + gaṛh ('fort'), rendered in-repo as Bîtâgar (replacing the 13th-century CE Kamatapur). Although the site's fortifications date to the 5th–6th century CE, its contemporary ancient name is unrecorded.

current_repo_state.name: Bîtâgar
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Kamatapur was founded in the mid-13th c. by Sandhya of Kamata; resolves via Option A to the 6th-c. fortified trade city Bhitagarh (Bîtâgar).

b_nalrajar_garh.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in government records in 1951 CE and surveyed by the Archaeological Survey of India in 1966–1967 CE as Nalrajar Garh (renamed Naranarayan Garh in 2025 CE).
b_nalrajar_garh.etymology_analysis: Bengali compound meaning 'Fort of King Nal', a modern folk designation for the Chilapata forest ruins (reattributed in 2025 CE to 16th-century CE Koch king Nara Narayan and renamed Naranarayan Garh).

b_bhitagarh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historical South Asian toponym; fictional/Germanic-style name in the repository state.
b_bhitagarh.etymology_analysis: Non-Indian Germanic-style compound ('meadow-abbey/foundation') present in current_repo_state.name for b_bhitagarh; not a historical pre-867 CE toponym in Bengal/Kamarupa.

b_cona_tibet.first_mention_attestation: Historical records of Tsona (Cona / Zône) begin in the 14th century CE (1354 CE); no datable pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_cona_tibet.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan mtsho-sna ('in front of / face of the lake', referring to Nara Yumco), rendered in-repo as Zône.

current_repo_state.name: Zône
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Zône).

b_nariyong.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; named after Nariyong Co (Lake Nariyong), the largest lake in Tsona County, Tibet.
b_nariyong.etymology_analysis: Tibetan hydronym designating Nariyong Co, a 58.33 sq km alpine lake in Tsona County, southeastern Tibet.

b_lhunze.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; Tibetan toponym Lhünzê (Lhun-rtse / Lhöntse Dzong) in Shannan, Tibet.
b_lhunze.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan lhun-rtse ('self-existing peak'), rendered in-repo as Lünzê.

current_repo_state.name: Lünzê
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Lünzê).

b_yumai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; Tibetan township name Yümai (Yul-smad / Yume) in Lhünzê County, Tibet.
b_yumai.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan yul-smad ('lower country/village'), a remote Himalayan valley township in the Tsari region of Lhünzê County.

b_tawang.first_mention_attestation: Attested from 1681 CE with the founding of Tawang Monastery by Merak Lama Lodre Gyatso.
b_tawang.etymology_analysis: From Tibetan Rta-dbang ('chosen by horse'), referring to the legend that Merak Lama's horse selected the site for Tawang Monastery in 1681 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Tawang
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tawang).

b_morshing.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; Monpa village in West Kameng, Arunachal Pradesh, near Lhagyala Monastery (17th century CE, with local tradition of a 7th-century CE foundation).
b_morshing.etymology_analysis: Monpa settlement name in West Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh (rendered in-repo as Morsching).

b_sepla.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; modern Seppa, administrative headquarters of East Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh.
b_sepla.etymology_analysis: Nyishi toponym (modern Seppa) referring to marshy ground along the Kameng River in East Kameng district, Arunachal Pradesh.

b_dimapur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; the Dimasa Kachari capital at Dimapur on the Dhansiri River dates from the 10th–13th century CE (sacked by Ahoms in 1526 CE).
b_dimapur.etymology_analysis: Assamese river hydronym Dhansiri (rendered in-repo as Dansîri), flowing past Dimapur (Dimasa Dima 'big river' + Sanskritized pura 'city').

b_herombial.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; medieval Assamese/Kachari ethnonymic/regional term for the Dimasa Kacharis of the Doyang-Dhansiri valley (Sanskritized as Hidimba / Heramba).
b_herombial.etymology_analysis: Assamese derivative from Heramba/Hiḍimbā, the Brahminical Sanskritization of the Dimasa Kachari kingdom in the Doyang-Dhansiri valley.

b_maibong.first_mention_attestation: Became the capital of the Dimasa Kachari Kingdom in the 16th century CE (c. 1536 CE after the Ahom sack of Dimapur).
b_maibong.etymology_analysis: From Dimasa mai ('rice') + bang ('much/abundant'), meaning 'land of abundant rice', serving as the Dimasa capital from the 16th to 18th century CE.

b_oddiyana2.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Oḍḍiyāna / Uḍḍiyāna in early Vajrayana Buddhist Tantric literature by the 7th–8th century CE (e.g., Indrabhuti's Jñānasiddhi and early Shakta pitha lists).

morphemes.translation: sacred Tantric realm/pitha (etymologized as 'flying/soaring' or 'garden' Udyāna)

b_oddiyana2.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Tantric toponym (Oḍḍiyāna / Uḍḍiyāna), historically centered in the Swat Valley (though some eastern Tantric traditions also associate it with Odisha or Assam).

b_goalpara.first_mention_attestation: Documented in early modern/colonial records (came under British East India Company rule in 1765 CE); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_goalpara.etymology_analysis: From Assamese gowāl ('milkman') + pārā ('neighbourhood'), traditionally derived from Gwaltippika ('village of the milkmen').

current_repo_state.name: Gôalpâra
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Constituent capital seat disambiguated from Kamakhya.

b_sri_surya_pahar.first_mention_attestation: Archaeological remains at the site date from c. 200 BCE and the 9th–12th century CE, but the modern Assamese/Hindi name Sri Surya Pahar has no datable pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_sri_surya_pahar.etymology_analysis: Assamese/Sanskritic compound meaning 'Illustrious Sun Hill', named for the sacred hill near Goalpara containing Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain rock-cut sculptures.

current_repo_state.name: Sri Surya Pahar
current_repo_state.b_origin: Sri Surya Pahar (constituent holding of Kamâkje)

b_kamakhya.first_mention_attestation: First explicitly attested as Kāmākhyā in the Kālikā Purāṇa (c. 10th–11th century CE, c. 950 CE); the 9th-century CE Tezpur copperplate of Vanamalavarmadeva (r. c. 835–865 CE) names the hill Kāmakūṭa and the deities Kāmeśvara and Mahāgaurī rather than the toponym Kāmākhyā itself.
b_kamakhya.etymology_analysis: Sanskritized as Kāmākhyā ('she who is named after desire'), widely traced by linguists (e.g., B. K. Kakati) to a pre-Aryan/Khasi goddess name such as Ka Meikha ('old-cousin-mother').

current_repo_state.name: Kamâkje
current_repo_state.b_origin: Kamakhya (ancient sacred Kamarupa hill shrine of Kamakhya) (in-game: Kamâkje)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Ancient sacred Kamarupa temple shrine Kamakhya.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Tezpur copperplate inscription of Vanamalavarmadeva (r. c. 835–865 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Vanamalavarmadeva's 9th-century CE Tezpur plate names the hill Kāmakūṭa and the deities Kāmeśvara and Mahāgaurī (identified with Nilachal/Kamakhya), whereas the explicit form Kāmākhyā appears later in the Kālikā Purāṇa (c. 10th–11th century CE).

b_manipur.first_mention_attestation: The Sanskritized name Manipur was adopted in the 18th century CE (reign of Pamheiba / Garib Niwaz, r. 1709–1748 CE); earlier indigenous names were Kangleipak and Meeteileipak.
b_manipur.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Maṇipura ('City of Jewels'), adopted during the 18th-century CE Hinduization of the Ningthouja kingdom (previously known in Meitei as Kangleipak).

b_khoupum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; Rongmei/Naga valley settlement in Tamenglong/Noney district, Manipur.
b_khoupum.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Tibeto-Burman (Rongmei/Meitei) toponym for the Khoupum valley in western Manipur.

b_srihatta.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Śrīhaṭṭa in the 935 CE Paschimbhag copperplate inscription of Chandra king Srichandra.
b_srihatta.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Śrīhaṭṭa ('Illustrious Market'), the historical name of Sylhet in northeastern Bangladesh.

b_jangalbari.first_mention_attestation: Attested in late 16th-century CE Bengal history when Isa Khan captured Jangalbari Fort from Koch rulers (c. 1580–1597 CE, commonly dated 1585 CE).
b_jangalbari.etymology_analysis: Bengali compound jangal ('forest') + bāṛī ('house/estate'), meaning 'Forest Homestead/Stronghold', located in Kishoreganj District, Bangladesh.

b_habiganj.first_mention_attestation: Founded as Habibganj by Syed Habib Ullah of the Taraf zamindar family (post-15th century CE) and established as a British thana in 1790 CE.
b_habiganj.eponym_details: Named after Syed Habib Ullah (of the post-15th-century CE Syed zamindar dynasty of Taraf), who founded the market town as Habibganj.

morphemes.translation: personal name of Syed Habib Ullah

b_habiganj.etymology_analysis: Contracted from Habibganj (Syed Habib Ullah + Persian/Bengali ganj 'market'), named after its early modern founder in Sylhet Division, Bangladesh.

b_charaideo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; the Tai-Ahom name Patkai (Pat-kai) dates from after the Ahom migration across the range in the 13th century CE.
b_charaideo.etymology_analysis: From Tai-Ahom Pat-kai ('to cut a chicken', referring to an oath sworn on the mountain pass), applied to the Patkai Range on the Indo-Myanmar border (used in-repo as a pre-Ahom replacement for Charaideo).

current_repo_state.name: Patkâi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Charaideo (Che-Rai-Doi) was founded in 1253 by Ahom king Sukaphaa; resolves via pre-Ahom oronym Patkai Range (Patkâi).

b_carguya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-867 CE written sources; medieval/early modern Upper Assam settlement name (Charaigua / Charguya).
b_carguya.etymology_analysis: Regional Assamese settlement name in Upper Assam without pre-867 CE epigraphic or textual attestation.

b_patkai.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historical South Asian toponym; fictional/Germanic-style name in the repository state.
b_patkai.etymology_analysis: Non-Indian Germanic-style compound ('Clementia-town') present in current_repo_state.name for b_patkai; not a historical pre-867 CE toponym in Assam.

b_kundina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE sources for Assam; Kuṇḍina is an epic/Puranic name of Vidarbha later localized to Sadiya (on the Kundil River) by medieval Chutiya and Neo-Vaishnavite traditions.
b_kundina.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kuṇḍina, associated in the Mahabharata and Puranas with Vidarbha and later identified in Assamese tradition with Sadiya on the Kundil River.

b_tinsukia.first_mention_attestation: Established as Bengmara (earlier Changmai Pathar) in 1791 CE by Matak king Sarbananda Singha, later renamed Tinsukia.
b_tinsukia.etymology_analysis: From Assamese tini-kunīyā / tinsukīyā ('three-cornered'), named after the triangular Tinikunia pond dug in the 18th-century CE Matak capital Bengmara.

b_ghuguha_dol.first_mention_attestation: Early 18th-century CE brick temple in Dhemaji district, Assam; no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_ghuguha_dol.etymology_analysis: Assamese compound ending in dol ('temple'), designating an early 18th-century CE brick shrine in Dhemaji district, Assam.

b_kiranapura.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Kiraṇapura in the post-945 CE Maliyapundi copperplate grant of Eastern Chalukya king Amma II, recounting c. 880–890 CE campaigns involving Rashtrakuta Krishna II and Kalachuri Sankila.
b_kiranapura.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit Kiraṇapura ('City of Rays', modern Kirnapur in Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh).

b_lanjika.first_mention_attestation: Attested as Lanjika (modern Lanji, Balaghat district) under a branch of the Kalachuris of Ratnapura in the 12th century CE (with Lanji Fort built in the 12th century CE).
b_lanjika.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sanskritized form Lanjika of modern Lanji in Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, later listed as a mahal in the Ain-i-Akbari.

b_mungeli.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; town and district headquarters in Chhattisgarh (carved out of Bilaspur district in 2013 CE).
b_mungeli.etymology_analysis: Modern Chhattisgarhi/Hindi town name in Chhattisgarh without pre-867 CE attestation.

b_nandgram.first_mention_attestation: Recorded as the earlier name of Rajnandgaon, whose princely state capital was established c. 1830 CE (late 18th/early 19th century CE); no pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_nandgram.etymology_analysis: From Sanskrit/Hindi Nandagrāma ('Village of Nanda'), the earlier name of Rajnandgaon in Chhattisgarh.

b_sambalpur.first_mention_attestation: Established as Sambalpur in 1540 CE by Chauhan king Balaram Dev.
b_sambalpur.etymology_analysis: Named after the presiding goddess Samaleswari (Sambhal) + pur ('city'), founded in 1540 CE on the Mahanadi River.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Geographia mentions Sambalaka on the Manada (Mahanadi) River, identified with the Sambalpur area prior to Balaram Dev's 1540 CE founding of Sambalpur.

b_rajgangpur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in datable pre-867 CE written sources; modern industrial town in Sundargarh district, Odisha (formerly part of Gangpur State).
b_rajgangpur.etymology_analysis: Odia/Sanskritic compound meaning 'Royal Gangpur Town', located in Sundargarh district, Odisha.

b_bikramkhol.first_mention_attestation: 1933 CE (first documented by K. P. Jayaswal in 'The Vikramkhol Inscription', Indian Antiquary, vol. 62)
b_bikramkhol.etymology_analysis: From Odia Bikramkhol (also Vikramkhol), combining Bikram ('valor / Vikram') and khol ('cave, hollow'), referring to the sandstone rock shelter in Jharsuguda district containing prehistoric pictographic engravings first published in 1933 CE.

b_sripuri.first_mention_attestation: c. 500–550 CE (epigraphically attested as Śrīpura in 6th–8th century CE Sharabhapuriya copper-plate grants, e.g., Sudevaraja and Pravararaja, and subsequent Panduvamshi inscriptions; Samudragupta's earlier Allahabad Pillar inscription names Kosala rather than Śrīpura).
b_sripuri.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit compound Śrīpura ('auspicious city' / 'city of Śrī-Lakṣmī'), epigraphically attested as the royal capital of Dakṣiṇa Kosala in 6th–8th century CE Sharabhapuriya and Panduvamshi inscriptions (c. 500–550 CE onward).

b_rajiva_lochana.first_mention_attestation: 8th century CE (c. 700–740 CE; Rajim Stone Inscription of Nala king Vilasatunga, paleographically dated to the 8th century CE)
b_rajiva_lochana.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Rajiva-Lochana ('lotus-eyed'), an epithet of Vishnu and the presiding deity of the Rajiv Lochan Temple at Rajim, Chhattisgarh, attested in the 8th-century CE Nala inscription of Vilasatunga.

b_suvarnapura.first_mention_attestation: c. 882 CE (Vakratentali copper-plate grant of Somavamshi king Janmejaya I Mahabhavagupta, r. c. 882–922 CE, issued from Suvarnapura)
b_suvarnapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Suvarnapura ('golden city'), modern Sonepur / Subarnapur in western Odisha, first attested in late 9th-century CE copper-plate charters of the early Somavamshi ruler Janmejaya I.

b_yajatinagara.first_mention_attestation: c. 922–955 CE (copper-plate inscriptions of Somavamshi king Yayati I Mahashivagupta issued from Yayatinagara)
b_yajatinagara.eponym_details: Named after the Somavamshi king Yayati I (Mahashivagupta I, r. c. 922–955 CE), who renamed or established the capital as Yayatinagara ('city of Yayati').
b_yajatinagara.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Yayatinagara (rendered Yajatinagara, 'city of Yayati'), the Somavamshi royal capital named after King Yayati I (r. c. 922–955 CE).

b_vinitapura.first_mention_attestation: c. 892 CE (Patna Museum copper-plate charter of Somavamshi king Mahashivagupta Yayati I issued from Vinitapura)
b_vinitapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Vinitapura ('well-ordered city'), an early Somavamshi capital on the Mahanadi River (identified with modern Binika in Subarnapur district, Odisha), attested in late 9th-century CE Somavamshi copper plates.

b_ranipur.first_mention_attestation: Modern settlement name with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation (temple site surveyed by John Campbell in 1853 CE and J. D. Beglar in 1874–1876 CE)
b_ranipur.etymology_analysis: Odia/Indo-Aryan Ranipur ('queen's town'), part of the twin-village name Ranipur-Jharial in Balangir district, Odisha, famous for its 8th–10th century CE temples including the Chausath Yogini shrine.

b_barasuru.first_mention_attestation: 1060 CE (Barsur Telugu stone inscription of Chhindaka Naga king Jagadekabhushana and feudatory Chandraditya, Shaka 983)
b_barasuru.etymology_analysis: Historical form Barasuru (modern Barsur in Dantewada district, Chhattisgarh), derived locally from Balsuri and attested in 1060 CE Telugu inscriptions of the Chhindaka Naga dynasty.

b_malkangiri.first_mention_attestation: Modern town name with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation (historically referred to as Malikamardhangiri)
b_malkangiri.etymology_analysis: Odia toponym Malkangiri, contracted from historical Malikamardhangiri (or associated with the Malyavanta hills and Mallikeshvara), with giri meaning 'hill, mountain'.

b_chutur.first_mention_attestation: Modern village name in Chinturu taluka, Andhra Pradesh (bordering Odisha and Chhattisgarh), with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
b_chutur.etymology_analysis: Modern rural toponym Chutur (rendered Tschutur in repository), a village in Chinturu taluka near the tri-junction of Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh.

b_cakrakuta.first_mention_attestation: 1023 CE (Tirumalai inscription of Rajendra Chola I recording Sakkarakottam / Chakrakota, and Chhindaka Naga records from 1023 CE onward)
b_cakrakuta.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Cakrakuta / Chakrakota ('wheel fort' or 'discus stronghold'), the medieval kingdom of the Chhindaka Nagas in Bastar-Koraput, first attested in early 11th-century CE Chola and Naga inscriptions.

b_umerkote.first_mention_attestation: Modern town name in Nabarangpur district, Odisha, with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
b_umerkote.etymology_analysis: Odia toponym Umerkote (also Umarkot / Amarkot), combining a personal or local element Umer with kote ('fort, stronghold').

b_kanker.first_mention_attestation: 1166 CE (Kanker copper-plate inscriptions of Somavamshi ruler Pampa Raja / Bhupadeva, 1166–1186 CE)
b_kanker.etymology_analysis: Toponym Kanker in southern Chhattisgarh, traditionally linked to sage Kank or stony terrain (kankar), first attested in 12th-century CE Somavamshi copper-plate inscriptions.

b_mandasa.first_mention_attestation: c. 577 CE (Narasimhapalli copper-plate grant of Eastern Ganga king Hastivarman, Ganga year 79, recording Kalinganagara)
b_mandasa.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kalinganagara ('city of Kalinga'), the early Eastern Ganga capital (modern Mukhalingam in Srikakulam district, Andhra Pradesh), attested from the late 6th century CE.

b_kalinganagara.first_mention_attestation: Anomalous Germanicized placeholder name in the repository ('Wernhardstat') with no historical attestation
b_kalinganagara.etymology_analysis: Anomalous Germanicized repository name Wernhardstat ('Wernhard's town') assigned to the barony key b_kalinganagara, replacing the historical Sanskrit toponym Kalinganagara.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Narasimhapalli copper-plate grant of Eastern Ganga king Hastivarman (Ganga year 79, c. 577 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: The active repository name 'Wernhardstat' is an anomalous Germanicized label on b_kalinganagara; the historical Eastern Ganga capital Kalinganagara (modern Mukhalingam) is attested by c. 577 CE.

b_srikakulam.first_mention_attestation: Post-medieval town name (also Chicacole under Golconda Qutb Shahis in the 16th–17th centuries CE) with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
b_srikakulam.etymology_analysis: Telugu/Sanskrit Srikakulam (known as Chicacole in colonial records), associated with the Srikakuleswara shrine and later regional administration under the Golconda Qutb Shahis.

b_swetakapura.first_mention_attestation: Late 8th century CE (c. 756–786 CE; Ganjam copper-plate grant of Shvetaka Ganga ruler Jayavarmadeva as vassal of Bhauma-Kara king Shivakara I)
b_swetakapura.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Shvetaka-Mandala ('Swetaka province'), the realm of the collateral Shvetaka branch of the Eastern Gangas in northern Kalinga / Ganjam, attested in 8th-century CE copper-plate charters.

b_rayagada.first_mention_attestation: 1527–1531 CE (founded by King Vishwanath Dev Gajapati of the Suryavamsa dynasty of Nandapur)
b_rayagada.etymology_analysis: Odia Rayagada ('royal fort'), founded in the early 16th century CE (1527–1531 CE) by Vishwanath Dev Gajapati of Nandapur.

b_asurgarh.first_mention_attestation: Modern Odia name of an Iron Age / early historic fortified site (5th century BCE–5th century CE) with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation of the name Asurgarh
b_asurgarh.etymology_analysis: Odia Asurgarh ('fort of the Asuras', or locally derived from Asokagarh), a modern designation for the early historic fortified settlement in Kalahandi district, Odisha.

b_vizagipatam.first_mention_attestation: 1068 CE (Inscription No. 187 of 1893, recording Visakhapatnam under King Visakhavarma)
b_vizagipatam.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit/Telugu Visakhapatnam ('city of Visakha', anglicized as Vizagapatam), first documented in a 1068 CE inscription.

b_nandapur.first_mention_attestation: Medieval capital of the Silavamsa dynasty in the 14th century CE, with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
b_nandapur.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit/Odia Nandapur ('city of Nanda / joy'), a historic seat in Koraput district, Odisha, attested as the capital of the 14th-century CE Silavamsa rulers.

b_katak.first_mention_attestation: c. 913 CE (three copper-plate grants issued from Kataka in the 31st regnal year of Somavamshi king Janmejaya I, r. c. 882–922 CE)
b_katak.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Kataka ('royal camp, cantonment, fort'), modern Cuttack, first attested in early 10th-century CE Somavamshi grants and later made the Eastern Ganga capital c. 1135 CE.

b_bhubaneswar.first_mention_attestation: 1058 CE (Brahmeswara Temple inscription of Kolavati Devi, 18th regnal year of Somavamshi king Uddyotakeshari, referring to the Shaivite center)
b_bhubaneswar.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Tribhuvanesvara / Bhuvanesvara ('Lord of the Three Worlds', an epithet of Shiva), superseding the earlier name Ekamra / Ekambaka.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Vigraha dynasty copper-plate inscription dated Gupta year 280 (600 CE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Before adopting the name Bhubaneswar (from Tribhuvanesvara), the Old Town temple complex was attested as Ekambaka / Ekamra in a 600 CE Vigraha inscription.

b_konarak.first_mention_attestation: c. 1250 CE (construction of the Konark Sun Temple under Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I)
b_konarak.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Konarka ('corner sun'), referring to the Sun Temple of Surya built c. 1250 CE by Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I.

b_dhauli.first_mention_attestation: Modern Odia hill/village name with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation (site of Ashoka's c. 256 BCE Rock Edicts naming Tosali)
b_dhauli.etymology_analysis: Modern Odia toponym Dhauli (from Dhavali, 'white hill'), located near ancient Tosali where Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts were inscribed.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Separate Kalinga Edicts of Ashoka at Dhauli (c. 256 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ashoka's Dhauli Rock Edicts name the Mauryan administrative center Tosali (associated with the Dhauli-Sisupalgarh complex).

b_sakshigopal.first_mention_attestation: Late medieval / modern pilgrimage town name (associated with Gajapati Purushottama Deva, late 15th century CE) with no datable pre-867 CE attestation
b_sakshigopal.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit/Odia Sakshigopala ('witness Gopal', i.e., Krishna as witness), the deity of the Sakhigopal Temple in Puri district, Odisha (formerly called Satyabadi).

b_athgarh.first_mention_attestation: 1178 CE (foundation of Athgarh State by Raja Srikaran Niladri Bebarta Patnaik)
b_athgarh.etymology_analysis: Odia Athagada / Athgarh ('eight forts'), the capital of the former Athgarh princely state founded in 1178 CE.

b_khijjinga.first_mention_attestation: 924 CE (Bamanghaty copper-plate inscription of Adi-Bhanja ruler Ranabhanja, dated year 188)
b_khijjinga.etymology_analysis: Sanskrit Khijjingakota ('fort of Khijjinga', modern Khiching in Mayurbhanj district, Odisha), capital of the Adi-Bhanja dynasty, first firmly dated in the 924 CE Bamanghaty charter.

b_asanapat.first_mention_attestation: Modern village name in Keonjhar district, Odisha (site of the 4th-century CE Nataraja stone inscription of Naga ruler Satrubhanja, published in 1965 CE) with no datable pre-867 CE attestation of the village name itself
b_asanapat.etymology_analysis: Modern Odia village name Asanapat in Keonjhar district, Odisha, where the 4th-century CE Sanskrit stone inscription of Naga king Satrubhanja was discovered.

b_bahalda.first_mention_attestation: Medieval Mayurbhanj capital in the 13th–14th centuries CE with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
b_bahalda.etymology_analysis: Regional Odia/Munda toponym Bahalda in Mayurbhanj district, Odisha, which served as a capital of the Mayurbhanj Bhanjas in the 13th–14th centuries CE.

b_ghatagaon.first_mention_attestation: Late medieval / modern town name in Keonjhar district, Odisha (associated with the Maa Tarini shrine, traditionally dated 15th–17th century CE) with no datable pre-867 CE attestation
b_ghatagaon.etymology_analysis: Odia Ghatagaon ('village at the pass/ghat'), located in Kendujhar district, Odisha, famed for the Maa Tarini temple.

b_malayagiri.first_mention_attestation: Modern/traditional mountain peak name in Angul district, Odisha, with no datable pre-867 CE written attestation
